resources.string: How gastric chief cells help digest protein
A qualitative view of normal human stomach digestion, following pepsinogen from a chief cell to the first steps of protein breakdown. The cutaways, timing, and molecular shapes are schematic.
Find chief cells near the gland base
Fundic glands in the upper rounded part and body of the stomach open through pits into the stomach cavity. Chief cells are concentrated deep in these glands, toward the base.
A chief cell packages pepsinogen, an inactive precursor of pepsin, into secretory granules. The granules collect near the side that faces the gland lumen, opposite the nucleus.
Release pepsinogen into the gland lumen
Granule membranes fuse with the chief cell membrane facing the gland lumen. Pepsinogen is released into the lumen, the space inside the gland, while the granule membrane stays with the cell.
Nearby parietal cells, not chief cells, secrete the acid. In the acidic gland lumen, a piece is cleaved from pepsinogen, leaving the active enzyme pepsin.
Pepsin starts breaking down food protein
Gastric juice carries pepsin into the stomach cavity. There, pepsin cuts long dietary protein chains into shorter pieces called peptides. This begins protein digestion; it does not finish it.
